title: Legislative Primaries to Watch in August Elections
text: Key primary races could help decide which party controls both the state Assembly and Senate. The Wisconsin Assembly chamber. Elections in August and November will determine who fills these seats and those in the state Senate. (File photo by Melanie Conklin/Wisconsin Examiner) While Wisconsin’s governor’s race is drawing national attention, control of the state Legislature could determine whether the next governor can enact their agenda. Legislative primaries will shape the handful of Assembly and Senate races that could decide control next year. Republicans are seeking to defend their majorities, which they’ve held since 2011. Democrats are seeking to flip two Senate seats and five Assembly seats while maintaining all the seats they hold currently to win majorities in both chambers. The outcome will determine how much of the next governor’s agenda — from Medicaid expansion to tax cuts and investing in education — can become law. There is sparse polling on state legislative races, although a survey in July from Marquette Law School found that 46% of Wisconsin voters said they would vote for Democrats in legislative races, while 42% said they’d vote for Republicans. The poll could not deliver detailed information on specific districts at play. Republicans are gearing up financially to defend their majorities, with the Republican Assembly Campaign Committee reporting $6.5 million raised in the first half of the year and a total of $11.5 million cash-on-hand. The Committee to Elect a Republican Senate raised nearly $5 million and had $5.3 million on-hand. The bulk of that fundraising came from billionaires Diane Hendricks , who gave $2.5 million to RACC and $2 million to the Senate GOP committee, as well as Elizabeth Uihlein , who gave $3 million to the Assembly committee and $2 million to the Senate committee. The contributions have given the Republicans organizations deeper pockets than their Democratic counterparts. According to recent campaign finance reports, the State Senate Democratic Campaign Committee, the fundraising arm of the Senate Democratic caucus, raised about $2.8 million over the first six months of the year, while the Assembly Democratic Campaign Committee raised $3 million and ended with nearly $2.4 million cash-on-hand. The primary is scheduled for Aug. 11. Here are seven primary elections the Wisconsin Examiner is keeping an eye on in the lead-up to Election Day. The general election is Nov. 3. A four-way Republican primary is taking place in the race to replace Sen. André Jacque in Senate District 1, which represents Door and Kewaunee counties. Nic Cravillion is an Army combat veteran and small business owner from New Franken who is campaigning on lowering taxes and promoting “responsible spending” as well as expanding workforce and affordable housing opportunities. For the last five years, Cravillion has also worked as the district director for Jacque. He reported raising $75,911 and having $62,264 on hand — more than any of the other candidates — at the end of the period. He also reported taking out $62,100 in personal loans. Barbara Bittner serves as the chair of the Calumet County Republican Party. She is running to reduce property taxes, protect “parental rights,” get “tough on crime” and uphold the “sanctity of life and traditional values.” Bittner reported raising $17,180.00 and having about $16,945 on hand at the end of the period. Katie Baney , a De Pere mother, currently works as the managing director of government affairs at Delta Defense, where she advocates for gun owners, and promises not to support any legislation that restricts the Second Amendment, according to her campaign website. Baney reported in July raising $46,772 and having $43,662 on-hand. Jacob VandenPlas , a veteran and farmer who founded DC Farm for Vets, a rehabilitation farm that provides education and services to veterans entering agriculture. No Democrat is running for the seat in the red-leaning district, though the winner of the Republican primary will face Mark Becker , a small business owner who was formerly the chair of the Brown County Republican Party and is now running as an independent. Becker left the party after Trump’s election in 2016 due to disagreements over the direction of the GOP. He reported raising $20,233 and having $15,078 cash-on-hand. He has received contributions from Adam Kinzinger , the former Republican Congressman from Illinois who left the party due to his opposition to Trump, and the campaign account of state Sen. Kristin Dassler-Alfheim (D-Appleton). Three Democrats are competing to win a spot on the ballot to take on Sen. Howard Marklein (R-Spring Green) in November. Marklein was first elected to the Senate in 2014, and has been the co-chair of the powerful Joint Finance Committee since 2021. The district includes Crawford, Grant, Green, Iowa and LaFayette counties as well as the southwestern corner of Dane County . Marklein won the district with 60% of the vote in 2022, but Senate District 17 changed considerably under the new maps. The district leaned Democratic by 1 percentage point in the 2024 presidential election and by over 4 percentage points in the 2024 U.S. Senate race, according to an analysis by John Johnson , a fellow at Marquette Law School. Marklein’s incumbency status gives him an advantage in the district, and he is also raising more than the other Democratic candidates combined. In his most recent campaign finance reports, Marklein reported raising $300,195 and ending the reporting period with $1.01 million in the bank. He received $100,000 — or about a third of his total contributions — from the Committee to Elect a Republican Senate . Rep. Jenna Jacobson (D-Oregon), who has served in the state Assembly since 2023, launched her campaign for the Senate seat in July 2025 with the backing of the State Senate Democratic Campaign Committee. The endorsement has provided her some advantages over her opponents, as she has campaigned with current Senators, including Senate Minority Leader Dianne Hesselbein , and received financial assistance from the SSDC. According to her latest campaign finance reports, Jacobson has raised about $109,277 and has about $201,177 in the bank. About $45,450 of her total contributions this year came from in-kind contributions from the SSDC in the form of campaign staff. title: City of Madison removes encampment - In Business Madison
text: City of Madison crews removed the protest encampment at the intersection of Baldwin and Williamson streets early Tuesday morning. In a statement explaining the decision for the removal, Madison Mayor Satya Rhodes-Conway decried the lack of focus on the original subject of the protest — Corey Ruiz, the 38-year-old Madison man who was fatally shot by a Madison police officer — and said an “illegal occupation” of the streets is not the way to solve complex systemic issues. In an Aug. 3 letter to the community, Rhodes-Conway said she is “deeply troubled” that Ruiz is no longer at the center of the current crisis the city faces. “We’ve provided the time and space to allow the community to grieve Corey and the loss of other community members by police hands in the Marquette neighborhood,” she wrote. “We hope to work with Corey’s family and the community to continue to have a space for people to visit a memorial. “Plans for a permanent memorial cannot be made until the occupation ends.” Ruiz was fatally shot on July 22 during an attempted arrest at the intersection. As the protest unfolded, complaints by residents and businesses mounted, and with public health and safety being undermined, the situation became unsustainable, the mayor contends. An investigation into whether the officer was justified in using deadly force continues at the state and local levels. The full text of Rhodes-Conway’s Aug. 3 letter to the community is as follows: “For almost two weeks now, City of Madison staff and elected leaders have been on the ground and communicating to and through community leaders to peacefully resolve extremely complex, emotionally fraught circumstances that started with the police taking the life of Corey Ruiz. Countless efforts have been made to convince people that the occupation of Williamson Street and Baldwin Street is counterproductive. A huge amount of patience has been given because the last thing Madison needs is a large-scale police operation. That’s why those occupying the area need to leave immediately. I’m deeply troubled that Corey is largely no longer at the center of the current crisis our city faces. We’ve provided the time and space to allow the community to grieve Corey and the loss of other community members by police hands in the Marquette neighborhood. We hope to work with Corey’s family and the community to continue to have a space for people to visit a memorial. Plans for a permanent memorial cannot be made until the occupation ends. There are too many residents and local businesses suffering because of the occupation, and it’s become increasingly clear that unsheltered people are being used as leverage for demands that, frankly, the City of Madison cannot deliver because we do not have the power to deliver them. As we and others have repeatedly explained, the City cannot make an arrest or bring criminal charges — that authority rests with the Dane County District Attorney following an independent investigation by the Wisconsin Department of Justice. The City does not control this timeline. I’m increasingly alarmed that those supporting the occupation at the intersection of Williamson Street and Baldwin Street are either purposefully ignoring the harm being done, or deliberately hoping that the situation spirals further out of control. The City has already issued tow notices to vehicles blocking the intersection, and citations and impoundment will follow. At no point did the City pay for porta-potties, and the company that supplied them has been asked to remove them or risk being cited and fined. For those concerned for our unsheltered neighbors and friends, enabling the illegal occupation of city streets is not helping. The City cannot — alone — solve our nation’s failure to provide for people’s basic needs. The faith community, nonprofits already engaged in this work, and individual community members can help the City and the County combat homelessness. But it is naive to think such a systemic problem can be solved overnight, or that maintaining an encampment in the middle of a street will do anything to hasten a solution. As we have outlined in past messages, efforts to provide services to the unsheltered currently at the site are being made by outreach workers and Community Development Division staff. Those suggesting this is a safe location for a homeless encampment are wrong and are actively inviting more trauma and harm. Please join us in finding long-term solutions. title: Police clear encampment on Williamson and Baldwin streets in Madison - Spectrum News
text: MADISON, Wis. — Police cleared the encampment on Williamson Street and Baldwin Street on Tuesday morning. The occupation of the streets began after police shot and killed Corey Ruiz less than two weeks ago. Authorities came in with bobcats and other heavy machinery to begin clearing barricades, furniture and tents at the site around 4:30 a.m. The city said it did not want to get law enforcement involved but some protesters refused to clear, with some throwing objects at vehicles and lighting fires in the street. That's when the Madison Police Department stepping in. It corralled protesters in the center of the intersection and arrested several people who were trying to prevent the memorial for Ruiz from being taken down. According to the city, the streets were officially back open as of 9 a.m. All city barricades and signage were removed from the area. Supporters of the encampment and memorial criticized the city for how the entire situation was handled. “They could have just been direct and said we’re going to give you 48 hours to move out and then everybody could’ve been given a timeline, nobody was ever given a clear timeline, all they kept doing was throwing vouches, hotel vouchers at the houseless community, less than half of the people here were houseless," said Shadayra Kilfoy-Flores. The latest development comes after Mayor Satya Rhodes-Conway called for an end to the encampment, with leaders saying a peaceful end was the best path forward. Rhodes-Conway issued a new video message on Tuesday following the encampment being cleared. She said the city is fully cooperating with the investigation. "As soon as we are allowed to under state law, the police department will provide all relevant materials to the Office of the Independent Monitor for their investigation,” she said, addressing claims last week by the Monitor that MPD was not cooperating with turning over materials. The mayor said the decision to clear the encampment was not made lightly, but there was much to consider, with local businesses and residents caught in the middle of what she called "an increasingly volatile situation." "I ask that if you truly care about building a better future, you allow local businesses to stay open, residents to freely access their homes, and the intersection of Williamson and Baldwin Streets to stay open. Let's focus our energy on the hard work of sustainable change. Holding government accountable for progress should not mean harming the community we all share," she said in the video. Police remained at the scene on Tuesday. The city has also sectioned off a portion of the sidewalk on Baldwin Street as a designated memorial site for Ruiz. The city said those looking to pick up their belongings could do so at the parking lot of Demetral Park; city staff will be there until midnight. As of Tuesday afternoon, about one third of the items had been picked up. Kaitlynn Rouse was one of several people who helps people sift through the various items taken from the encampment. She said she thinks what the city did Tuesday showed a lack of respect.  “I think there should have been a lot more care and empathy when it came to, at the very least, the people and the people’s resources and items," she said. Both Rouse and Kilfoy-Flores said this was just another example of the growing rift between city leaders and the people of Madison. “They’re against the community members who are grieving, in pain, and just seeing it as a nuisance instead of people who just care about their community," said Rouse. "We were starting to get past the anger part, and then there’s healing, but now we’re back to square one,” said Kilfoy-Flores. While the encampment may be gone, protesters said they won't stop fighting for accountability in Ruiz's death.

text: UPDATE 8/4/26 at 4:00p.m. – Protestors have returned to the intersection of Willy and Baldwin Streets in Madison hours after police had cleared out the encampment in the street. MADISON, Wis. – A protest encampment blocking off a Madison intersection for nearly two weeks is cleared for traffic once again. But those occupying the site at Willy and Baldwin Streets where police last month shot and killed 38-year-old Corey Ruiz did not leave quietly. title: Video Message from Mayor Rhodes-Conway - City of Madison, WI
text: For Immediate Release August 4, 2026 "Good morning, I'm Madison Mayor Satya Rhodes-Conway.  I want to start by saying that the death of Corey Ruiz is, tragically, another wake up call for Madison. Even one community member killed during interactions with the police is too many. The grief, anger, and frustration are real and I feel it, too. I want to be clear that the City is fully cooperating with the independent investigation conducted by the Wisconsin Department of Justice, and will respect whatever decisions the District Attorney makes regarding charges for the officers involved. As soon as we are allowed to under state law, the police department will provide all relevant materials to the Office of the Independent Monitor for their investigation.   There is more work to be done at the City level to prevent this from happening again - work to build on the success of our CARES program in diverting calls away from police, work on police policy and training, and more. We need reform at the state level as well. I know it's unsatisfying to hear that change takes time, and that these investigations and processes require patience. But these things do take time and many of the changes needed are not in City government's control.   For nearly two weeks, I and City staff have been working day and night to peacefully resolve the occupation of Williamson and Baldwin without law enforcement intervention. The City has committed to maintaining space for members of the community to gather and grieve, and we stand ready to do that work in collaboration with the family and the community. But that work could not begin while city streets were occupied, local businesses were on the verge of closing, and residents in the Marquette neighborhood were caught in the middle of an increasingly volatile situation.   A challenge of the last two weeks was that there was not one leader, one group, or one coalition that represented the people occupying the intersection. What is deeply regrettable is that many vulnerable people were caught in the middle, which is why the City spent considerable time and effort finding emergency solutions — efforts that succeeded in helping dozens of unsheltered people and families. We were doing this work before the occupation, and we will continue to do this work moving forward.  This morning, the City of Madison opened the intersection of Williamson and Baldwin. The work was led by non-law enforcement staff from multiple City agencies. Our goal was to clear the barricades, preserve personal belongings and memorial materials, and open the street up to normal traffic. The CARES Team and members of the Violence Prevention Unit were there from the beginning to assist.  Unfortunately, as City staff cleared the area, rocks and other items were thrown at City employees and two fires were set; as a result, law enforcement was called in to stabilize the scene, and a small number of individuals were arrested. Again, multiple efforts and calls to end the occupation peacefully were made but ultimately ignored.  The 50 or so unsheltered individuals who were onsite were given the option to stay in hotels and were offered transportation there. A significant majority decided to do so and around 10 people were also placed in hotel rooms yesterday. This effort was done with as much compassion as possible under less-than-ideal circumstances. Those with personal belongings left at the site can pick them up at Demetral Field.   Again, the decision to invoke this option was not made lightly and was only made after almost two weeks of trying to resolve the situation peacefully, and voluntarily, with the people occupying the site.  There are many hard conversations to come and I look forward to us coming together as a community to have them. I ask that if you truly care about building a better future, you allow local businesses to stay open, residents to freely access their homes, and the intersection of Williamson and Baldwin Streets to stay open. Let's focus our energy on the hard work of sustainable change. Holding government accountable for progress should not mean harming the community we all share.   Thank you, Madison. We are a strong and compassionate community. Together, we can support each other. Together, we can work towards change. Together we can get through this. title: Editorial | Madison officers must wear body-worn cameras - captimes.com
text: The Cap Times is an independent newsroom. Sign up for the Opinion Roundup newsletter for weekly Madison and Wisconsin viewpoints. During a mayoral debate at the Madison Public Library in February 2023, Mayor Satya Rhodes-Conway and challenger Gloria Reyes butted heads on issues ranging from housing to public safety. Rhodes-Conway expressed doubts about body-worn cameras preventing both police misconduct and police violence then, and has continued to be indecisive on the matter. Reyes pushed for more urgency on the topic, telling the Cap Times at the time, “Some will say we cannot afford the implementation of body cameras. After watching the murder of Tyre Nichols, I say we can’t afford not to have them.” Nichols was beaten to death by five officers in Memphis a month earlier during a traffic stop. The gruesome footage captured by their body-worn cameras did not save Nichols, but it led to seven officers being fired and three suspended. It was also crucial in both state and federal trials years later. A year before that, on Feb. 3, 2022, state Department of Justice agents shot Quadren Wilson five times in the back on the east side of Madison. None of the agents involved wore body cameras and the Madison Police Department reported no city officers witnessed the shooting — facts that left more questions than answers and further drove a wedge between law enforcement and the community. Less shrouded in mystery is the death of Kevin Price by Fitchburg officer Peter Johnston. We know the nature of his death and every moment leading up to it upon the Fitchburg officers’ arrival at Price’s apartment. Media outlets, including the Cap Times , obtained footage from body-worn cameras and scrutinized every detail of the 40-minute encounter. Researchers who study use of force were able to review the videos and conclude the officers created a dangerous and fatal situation, even if, frustratingly, Dane County District Attorney Ismael Ozanne declined to file criminal charges against the officer. The city of Madison has dragged its feet for years on body-worn cameras, even after green-lighting a pilot program in April 2022. Then, last year in a 17-3 decision, the Madison City Council rejected a proposal to fund a body camera program. But in the aftermath of Corey Ruiz’s death, the only video evidence the Department of Justice has in its investigation comes from bystanders’ cellphone footage, which may not cover the angles necessary to fairly assess the details of what happened and where the knife was in the seconds before Ruiz’s death. We believe it’s incumbent on all City Council members and the mayor to make a decision on this crucial accountability tool. Madison remains one of the only major metropolitan cities in the United States to not require department-wide cameras. It’s high time to change that and to add one more layer of accountability and transparency to public safety.

text: The Cap Times is an independent newsroom serving Madison and Wisconsin. Sign up for the Morning Update to receive news in your inbox each morning. Layla Lowe said she had a dream early Tuesday that something was going to happen. She was sleeping at the encampment at the intersection of Williamson and South Baldwin streets with other protesters who have been there since the July 22 fatal police shooting of Corey Ruiz, 38. Lowe said she was on edge. Madison Mayor Satya Rhodes-Conway had been warning for days the encampment would need to be removed. Authorities arrived around 5 a.m. Tuesday and alerted people with a megaphone that they would start cleaning up the site and people could pack their own belongings, according to Madison police spokesperson Stephanie Fryer. Some protesters then started three fires and threw objects at city staff, she said. Bystander videos show a chaotic scene where protesters were arrested and officers used pepper spray while clearing the encampment. Uniforms identified the officers as Madison police and State Patrol officers. “It was scary,” Lowe said. “If these people want to stand here and protest, let them protest. Let them do what they want. You all took an innocent boy's life. He didn’t deserve that. He deserved his justice, though. And we’re going to get it, some way, somehow.” Madison police officers stand near the intersection of Williamson and South Baldwin streets following the removal of a memorial for Corey Ruiz on Tuesday. Fryer said 17 people were arrested and it was unclear how many people were pepper sprayed. Three people were injured in the clash: two protesters and one city employee. One of the protesters was taken to a hospital. The city employee suffered a “medical event” and was also taken to a hospital, Fryer said. Later, the Police Department clarified that 16 people were arrested and booked into the Dane County Jail, and 10 others were issued citations and released. By mid-morning, dozens of officers remained at the scene while belongings were being boxed up and loaded into trucks, and street sweepers began moving through the area. Spray paint and chalk writings were left behind on the streets, sidewalks and buildings. Some remnants of the encampment like food and belongings also remained. “Demetral Park” was written on the sides of some boxes. Fryer said the items were being taken to the park, about a mile north of the intersection, for individuals to retrieve. She said city officials went tent by tent and tried to package individuals' possessions together. City buses were on site Tuesday morning to give rides to people experiencing homelessness who had agreed to be part of a hotel voucher program, Fryer said. Two residents around 9:30 a.m. asked whether the city was distributing free bus passes to get off-site. City Council member Davy Mayer, who represents the area, said nearly 30 of the roughly 50 unsheltered individuals who had gathered at the encampment took the city up on its hotel voucher offer. By about 9 a.m., cars and bikes were once again traveling through the intersection. By early evening, the number of protesters had grown by the dozens. Equipped with signs, megaphones and some masks, the protesters occupied the four corners of the intersection, being kept to the sidewalks by police officers as cars drove through during rush hour. Tensions were high and some protesters splashed water on passing police cars and verbal altercations broke out. Protesters chanted, "We control the traffic." As the City Council met virtually for its regular meeting Tuesday night, a small group of protesters gathered outside the municipal building downtown. While city leaders initially supported barricading the intersection so people could mourn and protest Ruiz's death, they have increasingly raised concern about its safety and impact on the neighborhood in recent days. Tensions in the neighborhood were on display Tuesday morning. During an interview between a witness to the event and the Cap Times, a resident near the corner of Baldwin and Jenifer streets popped out of her door and said she was “sick of this” and asked that the conversations go “somewhere else” away from her yard. Several businesses displayed signs demanding justice for Corey Ruiz, and several dozen protestors remained at the site, chanting phrases including “What’s his name? Corey!” and “The whole damn system is guilty as hell.” On Saturday, Rhodes-Conway issued a statement saying the city was “preparing for a respectful transition” but didn’t indicate the encampment would be cleared Tuesday. On Sunday, the mayor said towing notices had been issued to vehicles blocking traffic. Madison Mayor Satya Rhodes-Conway issues a recorded video statement on Tuesday, Aug. 4, 2026, addressing the city's decision to clear out an e… Late Tuesday morning, Rhodes-Conway issued a new statement and a recorded video in which she said “there is more work to be done” to prevent future police shootings. “I know it’s unsatisfying to hear that change takes time, and that these investigations and processes require patience,” the mayor said. “But these things do take time and many of the changes needed are not in city government's control.” Rhodes-Conway said she and other city staff had been “working day and night to peacefully resolve the occupation of Williamson and Baldwin without law enforcement intervention,” but their efforts were stymied by a lack of a single person or organization to negotiate on behalf of protesters. Mayer shared a statement from the mayor's office to City Council members, which said the city couldn't provide a schedule publicly to clear the encampment because it would have “compromised the unprecedented amount of planning it took to avoid having law enforcement lead this action.” “We learned from 2020 (George Floyd protests in Madison) that when police are being protested, having the department at the frontlines produces even more negative outcomes,” the statement says. “Setting a deadline or timeline for this action would have made keeping law enforcement away impossible.” A Madison police officer stands near the site as items from a memorial for Corey Ruiz are removed Tuesday. As officers stood at the intersection Tuesday, some residents shouted “it's not over” and “we will be back.” Protesters had been discussing ways to shrink the memorial so the protest could continue and the intersection could reopen, according to Ashzianna Alexander, a protester who left the encampment minutes before city officials arrived and returned later. “We wanted it to be peaceful, and you all chose chaos,” Alexander said. Protesters previously called for city leaders to dedicate an official memorial to Ruiz, assist in transporting belongings and resources to temporary housing elsewhere, and coordinate city resources that could help with the transition. Both Alexander and Basel said they hope protesters continue to apply pressure on officials. Wisconsin State Patrol officers stand nearby as city workers remove items Tuesday from a memorial for Corey Ruiz at Williamson Street and South Baldwin Street. Hanah Jon Taylor, owner of Cafe Coda along Willy Street, had backed those gathered at the intersection. Taylor, 76, said his support was in solidarity with “people who are fighting against the same type of legitimate police brutality and killings” as he saw growing up in Chicago. “I don't believe that there's such a thing as justifiable homicide,” Taylor said. “Especially when you're supposed to have the training and the experience to deal with somebody with a knife.” He decried the shooting of Ruiz, saying police should have seen and treated him as “a neighbor” rather than “the enemy” after being called to the area July 22 on a report that a person was looking into cars along the street. “I work with a lot of kids, and the first thing you learn as an educator is there's no such thing as a bad child,” he said. Disproportionate treatment of communities of color will continue, he said, without a broader cultural shift alongside police reforms. “Everybody seems to be expecting someone else to do something about it, other than white people. White people should be talking to white people,” Taylor said. “My kids want to get along with your kids. Police Chief John Patterson has said Ruiz was shot during a struggle to arrest him and the officer who shot Ruiz had been injured by a knife. The struggle and shooting were recorded on video by bystanders, and then spread on social media, drawing national attention and immediate protests. Rhodes-Conway has questioned the shooting, while City Council President Sabrina Madison and protesters have called for the officer’s arrest. title: How the charity behind Madison, Wisconsin’s ‘autonomous zone’ raked in taxpayer money - Washington Examiner
text: A Wisconsin nonprofit group leading an illegal protest encampment that blocked traffic enjoys lavish federal, state, and local funding. The city of Madison awarded Freedom Inc. at least $149,/000 this year for initiatives such as “[Southeast Asian] and Black Youth Programs” after years of similar community-focused grants , records show. The city’s awards offer a glimpse of the more than $5 million in government funds that flowed to Freedom Inc. since 2020, including from the Department of Justice and state officials. Madison Mayor Satya Rhodes-Conway is now condemning protesters reacting to a July police shooting after they camped out in the street for days, forcing shuttered businesses to lose money and emergency vehicles to detour. Online posts from those involved show Freedom Inc. pitching a tent inside the so-called “autonomous zone,” handing out supplies to protesters, and forming their “demands” to the city for policy change, the Washington Examiner reported. The city cleared the encampment on Tuesday morning after Rhodes-Conway spent days pleading with protesters to disperse on their own, according to media reports and Rhodes-Conway’s Tuesday comments . Rioters threw rocks and other debris at city workers during the dispersal, leading to “a small number” of arrests, she said. “Again, multiple efforts and calls to end the occupation peacefully were made but ultimately ignored,” the mayor said. Freedom Inc. stood firm on Tuesday, posting a joint Instagram post with other groups that declared “shame” on the arresting officers. The charity is organizing a “Mass Mobilization” protest for Tuesday evening at Wisconsin’s state capitol in Madison. Rhodes-Conway’s office and Freedom Inc. did not respond to the Washington Examiner’s requests for comment. Madison requires funding recipients to sign contracts explaining that they will comply with all relevant laws, ordinances, and regulations. Freedom Inc. is not currently accused of illegal activity. The Madison protests happened against the backdrop of a competitive Democratic primary election for governor on Aug. 11. Socialist candidate Francesca Hong , a state lawmaker who worked with Freedom Inc. on an education bill, told supporters in a July 22 statement that the group was “on the scene supporting community members” at the Madison demonstration. Like other leftist tax-exempt charities , Freedom Inc. attracts public funds for seemingly charitable programs while directing its overall resources toward political advocacy. The group described its mission in IRS filings as “to achieve social justice through coupling direct services with leadership development and community organizing.” Madison’s stated reasons for bankrolling Freedom Inc. since 2024 included “Older Adult Services,” “Family Strengthening” for black and Southeast Asian women, youth, and LGBT people, as well as a “Nkauj Hmoob Hmong Girls Group” and a “Black Girls Matter” program. Rhodes-Conway’s administration also announced $50,000 in 2020 for the nonprofit group to help foreigners overcome “obstacles such as immigration status and lack of documentation that prevent or make it more difficult” to obtain COVID-19 welfare funds. Former President Joe Biden’s DOJ also awarded Freedom Inc. $475,000 in 2024 “to enhance culturally specific services for victims of domestic violence, dating violence, sexual assault, and stalking,” federal records show. Between 2023 and 2026, Wisconsin’s Department of Justice awarded the charity hundreds of thousands of dollars in federal DOJ funds related to crime victim programs . Freedom Inc. reported a separate $548,863 from the state’s Department of Children and Families in 2020 for “Immigrant and Refugee” work, “Under-represented Populations,” “Pandemic Shelter,” and other purposes. The DOJ and the two Wisconsin departments did not respond to requests for comment. WHO’S BEHIND WISCONSIN’S ANTI-POLICE ‘AUTONOMOUS ZONE’ TAKING OVER CITY STREETS? Though Rhodes-Conway described the recent encampment as disorganized, Freedom Inc. assumed a leading role by hosting educational sessions, providing “abolish police” signs and other gear, and serving as a contact point for planning protest “actions,” according to activists’ online posts. Freedom Inc. also worked with the family of Corey Ruiz , who was killed in the July shooting, to write down and distribute demands that Madison defund its police, the Freedom Road Socialist Organization said. “OUR ONLY ENEMY IS THE STATE,” Freedom Inc. declared on Saturday during the encampment.

title: Mayor explains why police cleared Willy Street: ‘You cannot please everyone’ - The Cap Times
text: The Cap Times is an independent newsroom serving Madison and Wisconsin. Sign up for the Morning Update to receive news in your inbox each morning. In the two weeks since a Madison police officer fatally shot Corey Ruiz, Mayor Satya Rhodes-Conway said she’s heard from many community members with differing opinions about how the city should respond to the vigil and encampment that formed at the intersection where Ruiz was shot. At a press conference Wednesday, Rhodes-Conway said some residents wished the city had “come in on day one and stopped all the protests,” never allowing an encampment to form at Williamson and South Baldwin streets. Others wanted the city to allow the encampment to “go on for months and months and months.” A day after city officials and law enforcement decided to clear the intersection, Rhodes-Conway said there are “a lot of people who don’t think that we’ve done the right thing, but they all think that we’ve done the wrong thing for different reasons.” “I think few folks recognize the constraints that we operate under,” she said. “This is part of the business of being in government. You cannot please everyone, and so we collectively have to do our best to, yes, listen to our community, but also make the best decisions we can in the moment with the information that we have, prioritizing following the law, public safety, and then trying to do the best we can to take care of our community.” The press conference marked the mayor’s first after authorities removed the encampment . Police reported arresting or citing dozens of people as the intersection was being cleared. After protesters returned to the intersection Tuesday evening and began to block it again, police returned and cleared it again, arresting more people into Wednesday morning, according to police . Police Chief John Patterson said 22 people were arrested from Tuesday morning to Wednesday morning, though he didn’t provide details of when people were arrested or the charges. There was also one minor arrested who had a firearm, Patterson said. Police Chief John Patterson said 22 people were arrested between Tuesday morning and Wednesday morning where police cleared out an encampment and subsequent protests where Corey Ruiz fatally was shot by a police officer on July 22. Ruiz’s family issued a statement Wednesday thanking protesters while noting they “did not organize or authorize” the encampment. Ruiz’s family said they aren’t affiliated with any particular group. They said individuals “do not need our approval to demand accountability.” "To the activists who have shown up for Corey, thank you. Keep fighting for justice, peacefully and together,” the family wrote. “We ask everyone at that corner (Williamson and Baldwin streets) and everyone wearing a badge to keep this peaceful. No one else should be hurt in Corey’s name.” City leaders initially allowed protesters to barricade the intersection after the July 22 shooting so people could mourn and protest, but they increasingly raised concern about its safety and impact on the neighborhood. Over the last week, Rhodes-Conway issued a series of escalating statements about the city's response to the encampment. On Aug. 1, she said the city was “preparing for a respectful transition” and the next day said towing notices had been issued to vehicles blocking traffic. Dozens of city officials, Madison police officers and Wisconsin State Patrol officers converged on the site around 5 a.m. Tuesday to clear the encampment and reopen the intersection to traffic. After a clash with protesters, the city announced the street opened at 9 a.m. Hours after Madison police fatally shot Corey Ruiz, community members gathered near Williamson Street and erected a memorial encampment. City officials moved memorial items off the street. Other belongings were packed up in boxes and taken to Demetral Park about a mile north for people to pick up. By 11:30 a.m. Tuesday, police reported arresting 16 people and booking them into the Dane County Jail, mostly on charges of unlawful assembly and obstructing a police officer. Ten other people were cited and released. “The decision to invoke this option was not made lightly and was only made after almost two weeks of trying to resolve the situation peacefully and voluntarily with the people occupying the site,” Rhodes-Conway said Wednesday. Asked what led the city to remove the encampment, the mayor said the decision came down to “a balance of resources available and the time to make the plans that we needed to make.” Rhodes-Conway said input from business owners in the area about the encampment’s impact “definitely was a factor.” “Perhaps even more importantly,” she added, residents’ concerns about “how unsafe the situation was” drove the city’s response. She said an “increasing number” of people experiencing homelessness were showing up at the site, noting they continued to come “even after we had provided some of them with other options,” such as hotel vouchers. Before officials cleared the encampment Tuesday, Rhodes-Conway said city staff provided emergency assistance to dozens of individuals at the site, adding “most people left voluntarily.” From the start of the encampment to its clearing, about 70 people accepted vouchers to local hotels from the city, Jim O’Keefe, the city’s community development director, said at the press conference. “I felt like when we tipped over into ‘we are now just attracting more and more folks who are experiencing homelessness to come camp in the middle of the street,’ it was clear that the situation was increasingly dangerous for everybody, and having a huge toll on the neighbors who are in the immediate vicinity,” Rhodes-Conway said. “And I felt like that was not something that could continue.” A Madison police officer stands near the site as items from a memorial for Corey Ruiz are removed Tuesday. Around 8 p.m. Tuesday, protesters regathered at Williamson and South Baldwin streets with tents, according to police. Rhodes-Conway said protesters “briefly” blocked traffic at the intersection and where East Washington Avenue intersects with South Baldwin Street during the night. Police left Williamson and South Baldwin streets at one point in the evening Tuesday in an “attempt to de-escalate the situation,” according to police . Protestors “emptied dumpsters and trash cans throughout the intersection, rendering it impassable,” and protesters set five fires in the streets, which were extinguished by the Fire Department, police said. Patterson said Wednesday he “overall” supported the way police handled the protests. He said officers at the site Tuesday “never used tear gas.” He was aware of one incident where an officer deployed pepper spray. “I think they maintained professionalism. They maintained discretion. Frankly, they showed de-escalation when appropriate,” the chief said. Patterson acknowledged trust with the Police Department is “very fragile right now” and said there is a “tremendous amount of work to do.” “I said this last year when I applied for this job. I think it's an incredible Police Department. I think it's filled with incredible people. But we're not perfect,” he said. “I identified some areas that I think we're going to make immediate progress on, hopefully, or immediate steps to do some restructuring to help us get there.” Police Chief John Patterson and Mayor Satya Rhodes-Conway spoke to reporters Wednesday morning for the first time since the city cleared the Willy Street encampment that formed where police fatally shot Corey Ruiz. Madison officers and other city employees had a physical altercation with Aeiramique Glass, the city’s interim independent police monitor, on Tuesday afternoon. The Police Department released drone footage of the encounter, which captures multiple officers surrounding Glass after she is grabbed by one officer as she turned away from them. Patterson said the altercation is being reviewed by investigators. In a video posted to social media and circulated by several local news outlets, Glass says after the encounter that “they've been wanting to do this to me” and “I will burn this city down.” The video appears to show blood on one of Glass’ hands. The attorney for the independent police monitor’s office told Madison 365 that Glass’ remark was a “figurative, idiomatic expression.” “It's disturbing any time a city employee is calling for violence,” Rhodes-Conway said Wednesday in response to Glass’ comments. “But as the (City Council) has made clear time and time again, they want that office to be independent of my office, and it is. So I think I would ask council leadership what they think the path forward is there.” The city’s Office of the Independent Monitor is overseen by the Police Civilian Oversight Board. The office provides oversight of police separate from that of the city’s Police and Fire Commission. Rhodes-Conway said the city is cooperating with a state Department of Justice investigation into Ruiz’s death and will fully cooperate with any investigation by the Office of the Independent Monitor. A few protesters were at Williamson and South Baldwin streets Wednesday morning with police officers nearby. Traffic was flowing through the intersection and remnants of the previous night were evident, including what appeared to be a large burn mark on the pavement near South Baldwin and Wilson streets. Patterson said police will continue to staff the intersection for “the foreseeable future.” “I’m hopeful that we’re not visible, or we don’t need to be visible,” Patterson said, noting the Police Department is working with city partners to have them “be at the forefront whenever possible.” “We recognize that to some people in the area, we are what's causing the agitation, our presence,” he added. “So we don’t want to do that.” The Cap Times welcomes tips from readers to help us inform our community. Email tips@captimes.com or visit captimes.com/tips for more options. Rhodes-Conway said the city will continue monitoring the intersection. People had until noon Wednesday to collect personal belongings at Demetral Park. Remaining items will be held by the city’s Parks Division and can be retrieved through the division’s typical process for lost belongings. Rhodes-Conway expressed a desire to coordinate with Ruiz’s family and community leaders on building another memorial site, noting the city has identified areas in a nearby parking lane. Ruiz’s family said in their statement that they welcomed a memorial that ”honors the man he was.” “Corey was quiet, soft-spoken and giving. He thought about other people before he thought about himself. He had a family who loved him. He was not alone in this world, and he was not without help,” the family wrote. “We ask that he not be reduced to a label he never carried.” While Rhodes-Conway emphasized she wanted to “center” the desire of Ruiz’s family first, she acknowledged a “broader community desire” to be a part of the next steps forward. The mayor said she is hearing “many conflicting things” from the community that she hopes the city can reconcile through continued conversations. “We have heard in my office from so many people expressing pain for so many different reasons. We hear you. I acknowledge that pain, and I just ask that we continue to work together in a peaceful way,” she said. “There is so much work to do to support each other in this community and to make a more just Madison and a more just society. I still believe that we will do better working together than causing more harm and destruction.”

During the evening and into the night, some people returned to the site, starting fires and clashing with law enforcement, according to dramatic video of the scenes posted on social media. “Many in this community are angry and grief-stricken over Corey Ruiz’s life being cut short by the police. Those feelings are completely legitimate, and I feel them, too,” Madison Mayor Satya Rhodes-Conway said at Wednesday’s press conference. “But as mayor of Madison, I will not condone or accept that the solution is to further divide our community by causing harm to your neighbors and local businesses, harassing bystanders or setting fires in city streets.” Rhodes-Conway said she and the city have weathered criticism from every side over how they have handled the presence of the encampment over nearly two weeks . The street where Ruiz, a 38-year-old Black man, was killed by police had been converted into a makeshift memorial with artwork and messages on the street, but also grew to include tents, grills and mattresses. “There are people who wish that we had come in on day one and stopped all of the protests and never let an encampment happen. And then there are people who wish that we would let that encampment go on for months and months and months,” she said. “There are a lot of people who don’t think that we’ve done the right thing, but they all think that we’ve done the wrong thing for different reasons.” Along with protesters, the site had also become a gathering point for people without housing. Jim O’Keefe, Madison’s Director of Community Development, said Wednesday that about 70 people had accepted city vouchers to stay in hotels for up to a week, and that the city had also provided transportation to hotels or other locations. Belongings from the encampment were brought to Demetral Park, on the city’s east side. The mayor said that items not claimed by Wednesday can be retrieved by going through the city parks department. Rhodes-Conway said that the city would continue to monitor the intersection and ensure traffic could continue back through the site unimpeded going forward. She also said the city is “ready to coordinate with Corey’s family” to establish a memorial to Ruiz. “We are absolutely committed to allowing space for some sort of memorial,” she said. “It just can’t be in the middle of the traffic lights.” On Wednesday afternoon, Ruiz’s family released a statement through civil rights attorney Ben Crump. “Our family did not organize or authorize the encampment at Williamson and Baldwin streets,” the family’s statement reads. They disavowed a statement circulated by some activists that purported to come from the family and included a list of demands, saying, “We were never asked, and we never agreed to the statement released in our name.” “The city cleared that intersection yesterday,” the statement concludes. “We ask everyone at that corner and everyone wearing a badge to keep this peaceful. No one else should be hurt in Corey’s name.” Video taken overnight show chaotic scenes over a few blocks. In one, a line of police officers in riot gear block off an intersection at East Washington, a major thoroughfare extending to Madison’s interstates. The Madison Fire Department responded to five fires , according to that agency, set around the intersection in city dumpsters and trash cans. At the start of Tuesday’s meeting of the Madison Common Council, Alder Barbara Harrington-McKinney asked if leaders could suspend the meeting and reconvene later “because there is craziness in the streets.” The meeting continued, with about eight hours of public comment while chaos raged on Williamson Street. No action was taken. Among those involved in altercations with police was the city’s interim police monitor, Aeiramique Glass. In drone video released by the city, she is seen confronting officers at the site. She appears to push one of them before a group of officers subdues her. In a social media video posted after the altercation, she shows a bloodied hand and says, “I will f—— burn this city down.” Rhodes-Conway on Wednesday called it “disturbing” for a city employee to call for violence. Patterson praised how his agency has handled the protests and ensuing flare-ups throughout the day and into the night. He said that neighboring Sun Prairie and the state police were also involved. Patterson said no tear gas or projectiles had been deployed and one officer used pepper spray. The protest zone was erected almost immediately after Ruiz was shot dead in the street, after being apprehended by police officers. Police say he brandished a knife, cutting one police officer, before he was killed. The shooting was captured on video, sparking days of community protest that culminated in a barricaded encampment on the commercial thoroughfare affectionately referred to as Willy Street. For days leading up to Tuesday’s clearance actions, Rhodes-Conway had been calling for an end to the encampment, which she said was straining local businesses and disrupting residents’ daily lives. On Wednesday, she said there was no inciting incident that made Tuesday the day. She said the city had tried to involve other agencies foremost, using police as a last resort. “Often the presence of police officers is part of the escalation, and so we have tried very hard to limit police response to what’s necessary and to use other city staff,” she said. Patterson said city agencies would “staff the intersection for the foreseeable future” to ensure that residents and businesses can return to regular life. “We recognize that for some people in the area, we are what’s causing agitation — our presence — and so we don’t want to do that,” Patterson said. Ruiz’s death is under investigation by the state Department of Justice. Separately, Madison operates an independent police oversight board, with an individual police monitor. Glass, the interim independent monitor involved in the altercation Tuesday, has called on the city to release its records to her office now, instead of after the DOJ investigation concludes. “I should not have to wait,” she said in a July 28 interview with WPR’s “ Wisconsin Today .” On Wednesday, Patterson said that’s not his call to make. “I’ve had discussions literally every single day, multiple times a day, with (the Division of Criminal Investigation) about what updates can be shared. … I’m assured they continue to progress in their investigation,” he said. “I feel it’s really my job to allow the investigating agency to do their work and make some of these decisions on records as well. I don’t want to be a chief that’s going to try to influence decisions one way or the other.” At Tuesday night’s city council meeting, Madison City Attorney Mike Haas said the city’s official position is that those records cannot be provided to the police monitor until the Wisconsin DOJ investigation is over. title: Madison police clear encampment at shooting site, arrest 16 - WXPR
text: This story comes from the  Wisconsin News Collaborative , a partnership of Wisconsin public media newsrooms, including WUWM, Wisconsin Public Radio, and WXPR. Madison police arrested 16 people Tuesday morning as officials moved to clear an encampment at the site where a Madison police officer shot Corey Ruiz on July 22 . The city released the latest arrest totals Tuesday evening. After city workers approached the encampment around 5 a.m. and some of those occupying the space did not leave, a police spokesperson said the demonstrators threw rocks and set fires. Police moved in, and the street reopened to traffic just after 9 a.m. For close to 13 days, the area had been blocked off by a memorial to Ruiz, a 38-year-old Black man. That memorial morphed into an encampment spanning several city blocks, as people brought tents, mattresses and grills to the site at South Baldwin and Williamson streets, known as Willy Street to Madison residents. After the street reopened, protesters attempted to block it intermittently throughout the day, a city spokesperson confirmed Tuesday evening. Traffic continued through the day, although demonstrators at times swarmed back into the intersection. By the time the sun was up Tuesday, garbage and city pick-up trucks were carting things away as police in riot gear stood by. Bulldozers and forklifts rolled through the street. Some residents watched from the sidewalk as officials worked to restore the intersection. A small group of protesters remained, with one person shouting through a bullhorn and some chanting, “No justice, no peace” and “no racist police.” The tents that had made up the encampment were gone. Around 8 a.m., city street sweepers moved in to clean the area. City workers placed memorial objects into boxes that were later taken to Demetral Field, a nearby park. Items include a sculpture of a raised fist that had been part of a memorial for George Floyd in Minneapolis and was brought to the Madison site. “For nearly two weeks, I and city staff have been working day and night to peacefully resolve the occupation of Williamson and Baldwin without law enforcement intervention,” Madison Mayor Satya-Rhodes Conway said in a video message on Tuesday , adding that city officials plan to work with the Ruiz family and other community members to create an ongoing space to grieve. “But that work could not begin while city streets were occupied, local businesses were on the verge of closing and residents in the Marquette neighborhood were caught in the middle of an increasingly volatile situation,” she added. Madison police officers stand in an intersection where a memorial for Corey Ruiz had been set up and maintained by protesters in an encampment Tuesday, Aug. 4, 2026, in Madison, Wis. The city used street sweepers to clean up the area and re-open it to traffic. Angela Major/WPR Madison Police Department spokesperson Stephanie Fryer told WPR the city initially sent in non-police staffers to tell people to clear the area. She said the city sent its Community Alternative Response Emergency Services or CARES team, and that street division workers walked through the encampment with a megaphone “essentially telling people now is the time to begin grabbing your belongings and leave.” Fryer said police got involved after people began starting fires and throwing objects at Streets Division workers. “We also had been told that they were taking candles that were lit for the memorial and also throwing those in the air, trying to start fire that way,” Fryer said. The mayor’s on update on Tuesday specifically mentioned two fires. It also said that people threw rocks. Two people protesting were injured while the encampment was being cleared, according to Fryer. One person was evaluated by medical staff and taken to the hospital with non-life-threatening injuries, and the other refused treatment. Fryer said a city employee was taken to the hospital after suffering a “medical event.” Fryer emphasized that no one’s personal property from the site was being thrown away. “The only things that were removed and actually thrown away were the items that obviously were started on fire or actual trash in the area,” Fryer said. Samuel Brooks of Portage was among those cited. He said he was handcuffed, given a court date and later released by police after being at the encampment early Tuesday. Brooks said he previously spent more than a decade living in the Willy Street neighborhood and had been at the encampment overnight. “We saw city vehicles moving around, and then we got word that the police were massing nearby, and yeah, they just circled up,” Brooks said. Brooks said city officials arrived some time before dawn. When that happened, he said he was among the people trying to wake up a homeless couple who were sleeping in a tent. “Bulldozer was coming straight for their tent,” Brooks said. “People were trying to get things under his wheels so we could get these people out of the way before they came through.” Protesters comfort each other as a memorial for Corey Ruiz, a man who was shot and killed by Madison police, is moved out of the intersection where the shooting occurred Tuesday, Aug. 4, 2026, in Madison, Wis. City workers and police also removed an encampment in the area. Angela Major/WPRBrooks’ citation report showed he was apprehended on suspicion of obstruction and resisting arrest. It listed a $449 fine from the city. He said he wasn’t worried about the citation. “I’ve got resources,” said Brooks, who is white. “I think my skin is a shield against police violence in a lot of situations.” Chaous Riddle of Madison said she was also at the encampment when it was forcibly cleared early Tuesday. “The whole thing was actually horrific,” Riddle said, as she recalled seeing heavy machinery and construction equipment plowing through the area. “They came in with their ToolCats. They barely missed people because it was dark.” In an update Sunday, Rhodes-Conway said the city partnered with local agencies to provide hotel vouchers to roughly  “25 to 30” who were homeless  and staying at the encampment. According to the mayor’s latest update , another 10 people were placed in hotel rooms on Monday. “The 50 or so unsheltered individuals who were onsite were given the option to stay in hotels and were offered transportation there. A significant majority decided to do so,” Rhodes-Conway said on Tuesday. “This effort was done with as much compassion as possible under less-than-ideal circumstances.” Alyse Weber of Madison lives just four blocks from where the encampment took place. For days, she says people were bringing items to the encampment, including food, electrolyte drinks, diapers and medical supplies. After the encampment was cleared, Weber broke down in tears as she described people looking through boxes for their items. “I was looking for my unhoused neighbors — people that I ignored, people that I’m sure my neighbors ignored out of fear of the unknown,” Weber said. “And, for the last two weeks, we’ve seen them and loved them, and been in community with them. And I certainly hope that part continues.” The encampment started as a protest site following the death of Ruiz in a struggle with police. It has blocked a busy thoroughfare and shut down traffic to businesses and residences in the neighborhood since. Police said Ruiz, who was homeless, produced a knife during a struggle with police, injuring one officer. Police used a Taser that they said was unsuccessful, and then an officer fatally shot Ruiz. The shooting, which was captured on video by bystanders, is being investigated by the state Department of Justice. Protesters have called for a permanent memorial to Ruiz as one of their demands following the shooting. Devon Snyder, a civil rights activist who is part of Madison’s Police Civilian Oversight Board, said he found the city’s move to clear the site “hypocritical.” “This is disheartening,” Snyder told a WPR reporter at the scene. “Something that was a tragedy, built a beautiful community. And they come and do this? … They want to call this an unlawful assembly. If this was an unlawful assembly, then why did the city support this for the last week?” Following the shooting of Ruiz, demonstrators dragged trash carts to block off the area. There were also homemade barriers around the encampment, including nails hammered into a strips of wood that was placed on the pavement. City officials also put up official barricades and announced on July 23 that the area of the encampment would be blocked off “until future notice.” At times throughout the last two week, the city has also parked salt tracks around the encampment to help block it off. A private company supplied port-a-potties to the site, and Rhodes-Conway has refuted reports that the city provided any portable toilets to the encampment. The move to clear the encampment comes after days of escalating warnings by Rhodes-Conway . On Sunday, she said the city would issue tow orders for vehicles blocking the street. On Monday, she signaled city action was imminent. “Countless efforts have been made to convince people that the occupation of Williamson Street and Baldwin Street is counterproductive,” Rhodes-Conway said in a statement Monday. “A huge amount of patience has been given because the last thing Madison needs is a large-scale police operation. That’s why those occupying the area need to leave immediately.”Kilfoy Flores, former chair of Madison’s Police Civilian Oversight Board, criticized the mayor for not being seen at the encampment before it was forcibly broken up. “I think that she should have come and mourned with her constituents,” Flores said. “Coming and mourning somebody’s death doesn’t mean that you’re choosing a side. It means that you’re coming to support your community who’s in pain.” Madison Alder Davy Mayer and Dane County Supervisor Yogesh Chawla were at Demetral Field on Tuesday morning as people sorted through boxes from the encampment. “They’re also being very careful because there were a large number of sharps found on site,” Mayer said. “So a lot of people have protective gloves that are going through things.” Mayer and Chawla represent the near east side neighborhood where Ruiz was shot. Chawla noted that rain could be coming and said there’s a plan to cover memorial items with tarps if that happens. “(We wanted) to make this difficult process as orderly and efficient and as compassionate as possible,” Chawla said. Mayer said he did not have an estimate early Tuesday of how much clean up would cost the neighborhood. After street sweepers went through, graffiti messages remained, including on sidewalks and the Baldwin Corners apartment building. Going forward, Mayer said the plan is to create a memorial not solely to Ruiz, but rather to “all the victims of police violence.” In addition to the killing of Ruiz, Madison’s Willy Street neighborhood has been the site of two other fatal shootings by police, one in 2012 and another in 2015.

text: MADISON, Wis. — The encampment on Madison's Williamson Street may be gone , but unrest continues in the city. Madison leaders came together for a press conference Wednesday two weeks after 38-year-old Corey Ruiz was shot and killed by a Madison police officer. Mayor Satya-Rhodes Conway said the feelings of anger by the community are legitimate, but she believes the “ illegal encampment ” that developed from Ruiz’s memorial was not the way to enact change. “I felt like when we tipped over into, we are now just attracting more and more folks who are experiencing homelessness to camp in the middle of the street, it became clear that the situation was becoming increasingly dangerous for everybody,” Rhodes-Conway said. The mayor said the intent of the city was to reach a peaceful and mutual end to the occupation . Rhodes-Conway said when that didn’t develop, the city moved to clear the encampment Tuesday morning without the use of law enforcement. She said police only got involved after protesters began throwing objects at city employees and lit multiple fires in the street. Police Chief John Patterson said protests continued late into the night Tuesday after the encampment was cleared, with 22 people being arrested at that time. Patterson said law enforcement presence will continue on Williamson Street for the foreseeable future, while also trying to give space to the community. “We recognize that for some people in the area, we are what’s causing agitation, and so we don’t want to do that,” Patterson said. “We’re trying very hard to work with our partners, city streets employees, parks employees, to have them be at the forefront whenever possible.” Looking back at everything that’s transpired over the last two weeks, Patterson acknowledged there’s a growing rift between the Madison Police Department and the people of Madison. “I feel like our trust is very fragile right now; we have a tremendous amount of work to do,” Patterson said. “I think this is an incredible police department, but we’re not perfect.” Rhodes-Conway said that distrust also extends from community members to city leadership. Zon Moua helped organize a protest outside the Dane County Public Safety Building Wednesday afternoon and called for city government to do better. “You’re not showing up for the community, you’re not doing what you’re supposed to do, you’re not actually putting money into actually making sure there’s care for the community,” Moua said. “You continue to invest money in harm; we are out here actually showing you and showing the community what it looks like when we keep ourselves safe and care for each other.” Rhodes-Conway said she understands why people have been critical of the city’s response to the last two weeks of protests. However, she’s standing by how leadership has handled what’s turned into a complex and delicate situation. “Everybody has an opinion on what we should do; I think few folks recognize the constraints we operate under,” Rhodes-Conway said. “There’s a lot of people who don’t think that we’ve done the right thing, but they all think we’ve done the wrong thing for different reasons. This is part of the business of being in government, you can’t please everybody, and so we collectively have to do our best to listen to our community but also make the best decisions we can in the moment with the information that we have.” Rhodes-Conway said the city is still committed to maintaining a memorial for Corey Ruiz in the Williamson Street area, as long as it does not impede businesses or neighbors. Chief Patterson said he’s in daily contact with the Department of Justice’s Division of Criminal Investigation and will share more information once their investigation into Ruiz’s death is complete.
